The posthoc sensitivity analyses are presented in the Supplement 2 . The findings of these analyses are that the 2 groups had similar clinical risk of PE (eTable 2 in Supplement 3 ). The noninferiority hypothesis remained confirmed in the per-protocol population, and the rate of CTPA was significantly reduced in the PERC group (eTable 3 in Supplement 3 ). Discussion

In this cluster-randomized trial of very low-risk patients with suspected PE, randomization to a PERC strategy vs conventional strategy did not result in an inferior rate of thromboembolic events over 3 months. In addition, the PERC strategy was associated with a benefit in terms of reduced CTPA use, ED length of stay, and likelihood of initial admission into hospital.

After initial validation on observational studies in the United States, the PERC rule has been challenged in Europe by 2 studies that reported an unacceptable rate (>5%) of PERC-negative patients with a PE diagnosis. One reason for the reported high prevalence of PE among PERC-negative patients could be the overall higher prevalence of PE in a European population. Another reason was that the authors used a structured score to evaluate the clinical probability (Wells or Geneva scores), which is made redundant when the PERC rule is used. One study reported better results when combining PERC with low gestalt clinical probability with no false negative of the PERC rule. The primary end point chosen, ie, the presence of PE after formal work up in the ED, can also explain in part the discrepancies, leading to a substantial rate of overdiagnosis, with a greater number of small PEs diagnosed that could be left untreated.

The end point chosen for the current study was a symptomatic pulmonary thromboembolism at 3 months and did not include the presence of a PE after formal work up in the ED. This could explain the difference of prevalence of PE described in the 2 groups (1.5% in the PERC group vs 2.7% in the control group; P = .052). The real PE prevalence in the PERC group may actually have been higher if all patients had undergone formal work up with D-dimer testing. It is very likely that some patients in the PERC group were discharged with a small untreated PE, which was not symptomatic even at 3-month follow-up. There was no significant difference in diagnostic yield of CTPA for PE (11% in both groups). A increased yield with the use of PERC might have been expected as has been reported with other clinical decision rules. However in this study, the small number of diagnosed PEs may have resulted in a lack of power to detect significant differences between the 2 groups. In the PERC group, there were fewer initial PEs diagnosed than in the usual care group, with little difference between the 2 groups in clinically significant thromboembolic events at 3 months. This suggests that PERC may be inferior at capturing low-risk events such as small subsegmental PE, with no clinical benefit in diagnosing the missed PEs in the PERC group. This may represent a tolerable risk to patient safety because small subsegmental PE can be left untreated. Another potential reason for the lower rate of PE in the PERC group may be that the 2 groups were not similar in their initial clinical probability of PE. In the posthoc sensitivity analyses with similar groups, the PE prevalence in the 2 groups was slightly modified (1.7% in the PERC group vs 2.7% in the control group in the first posthoc analysis and 1.5% in the PERC group vs 2.3% in the control group in the second posthoc analysis; eTable 4 in Supplement 3 ). However, this difference was no longer statistically significant.

Future research could evaluate the economic benefit of implementing PERC in routine practice. Furthermore, the safety and benefit of the modified PERC rule for patients younger than 35 years should be evaluated and compared to the initial PERC rule. Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, the observed prevalence of PE in patients with a low gestalt probability is very low. Although this category should include patients with a PE prevalence below 15%, only 26 patients (2.7%) in the control group were diagnosed with a PE in the ED. This corresponds with an overestimation of the risk of PE by the clinician’s gestalt, which has been described previously. The 2.7% prevalence (95% CI, 1.8% to 4.0%) reported here is below that reported in previous studies. However, similar PE prevalences for low-risk patients have also been reported in a recent study (pooled prevalence in the ED, 3.1% [1.0% in the United States and 4.3% outside of the United States]). Furthermore, among low-risk patients with chest pain or dyspnea, the reported prevalence of PE was 0.9%. In a recent large multicenter prospective study, Penaloza et al reported a prevalence of 4.7% (95% CI, 3.5% to 6.1%). The mean age of the patients was 44 years in this study, which is younger than in other main studies. This could partially explain the low prevalence of PE in this sample. Furthermore, a CTPA was defined as positive if it showed an isolated subsegmental PE. This could be considered controversial as these PEs could be left untreated.

Second, the failure rate of the diagnosis strategy in the control group was below the estimation, and therefore, the sample size calculation was not accurate. The 3% maximal failure rate that has been used in other trials is derived from studies published more than 15 years ago. Since this percentage is very large compared to the less than 1% of events rate recently reported, this raises the question of its validity. Recently, the Scientific and Standardization Committee of the International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis published a recommendation to decrease the maximal acceptable failure rate to 2%. With this new recommended threshold, the present results would still be valid.

Third, this was not a patient-level randomized trial, therefore a bias inherent to the cluster design cannot be excluded. This shortcoming is however partly limited by the absence of period and sequence order effects. Fourth, it is possible that an occult inclusion bias may have been introduced, in which emergency physicians were willing to discharge PERC-negative patients with no further testing and therefore did not include some of these patients in the trial during the control period. This could not be assessed because data were not recorded regarding the number of eligible patients who were not enrolled. The difference in the rate of PERC-negative patients and clinical probability of PE between the 2 groups ( Table 2 ) suggests that physicians could have included more very low-risk patients in the PERC group, as they were willing to discharge them with no further testing. However, 2 post-hoc sensitivity analyses confirmed the primary result of noninferiority, although with smaller effect on the secondary end points.

Fifth, there were 54 patients lost to follow-up and the presence of a few events among these patients would have altered the conclusion of this study. A worst-case scenario simulation would have led to the rejection of the noninferiority hypothesis (difference, 0.2% [upper bound of the 95% CI at 1.6% for a margin set at 1.5%]). Sixth, it is possible that the use of PERC induced diversion of unnecessary testing, and therefore patients not tested for PE were tested for another acute condition such as coronary syndrome. However, these data were not collected for these patients in this study. Conclusions

Among very low-risk patients with suspected PE, randomization to a PERC strategy vs conventional strategy did not result in an inferior rate of thromboembolic events over 3 months. These findings support safety of PERC for very low-risk patients presenting to the emergency department. Supplement 1. Trial Protocol Click here for additional data file. (2.5MB, pdf) Supplement 2. Patients with pulmonary embolism (PE) commonly manifest concomitant “pneumonia,” which is generally believed to be either a cause (infection) or a consequence (infarction) of PE. This study aimed to clarify the relationship between PE and “pneumonia‐like” lesions beyond pulmonary infection and infarction. Chest computed tomography (CT) images of patients with PE and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) were retrospectively analyzed to compare the incidence of pneumonia lesions. The pathological damage and wet/dry ratio of lung tissues were observed in PE rats and PE plasma‐injected rats. In total, 793 and 914 inpatients were enrolled in the PE and DVT groups, respectively. Pneumonia lesions were observed in 36.9% and 26.3% of patients in the PE and DVT groups, respectively ( p < 0.0001). Among PE rats, 33.3% exhibited focal severe lung injury, which closely resembled the pathological damage of community‐acquired pneumonia. The wet/dry ratio was significantly higher in the PE group than in the PE‐control group (4.98 ± 0.08 vs. 4.39 ± 0.06, p < 0.0001). Among PE plasma‐injected rats, individuals with focal proven lung injury were found at all experimental points, with an incidence of 27.6%. The lung wet/dry ratio was significantly higher in the PE plasma group than in the PE‐control plasma group at 1 and 2 h postinjection (5.02 ± 0.12 vs. 4.61 ± 0.06 and 4.76 ± 0.16 vs. 4.34 ± 0.09, respectively; p < 0.05). In conclusion, the manifestation of pneumonia lesions in chest CT images was higher among PE patients than among DVT patients. Plasma of PE rats could induce focal pneumonia‐like lung injury in healthy rats.

Keywords: computed tomography image, deep vein thrombosis, lung injury INTRODUCTION Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common disease with high mortality. 1 , 2 Pathogenic microbial infection is an important risk factor for PE. 3 Since the thromboembolus that causes PE originates from deep vein thrombosis (DVT), the incidence of pulmonary infection should theoretically be similar between DVT and PE. However, extant data have indicated that patients with pneumonia had a 7.9‐fold higher risk of PE but only a 3.0‐fold higher risk of DVT, 4 although patients with urinary tract infection had similar risks of DVT and PE. 3

Given that pulmonary infarction in PE might be incorrectly accounted for as “pneumonia,” resulting in false positives to raise the “pneumonia” incidence, should the “pneumonia” incidence in PE be so high? It is generally believed that pulmonary infarction in PE involves the occlusion of distal pulmonary arterioles due to thromboembolic blocking, resulting in ischemia, hemorrhage, and eventually necrosis of the corresponding lung parenchyma. 5 However, lung parenchyma damage caused by pulmonary infarction is rarely observed in precapillary pulmonary hypertension, which typically presents as pulmonary arteriolar occlusion in pathology. 6

This implies that the incidence of pulmonary infarction might not be so high even if patients with PE develop pulmonary arteriolar occlusion. We assume that patients with PE coexisting with pneumonia might have other confounding factors. Extensive evidence indicates that various inflammatory factors are activated and released in acute PE, including key pro‐inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor‐α (TNF‐α), interleukin (IL)−6, and IL‐8. 7 , 8 These inflammatory factors can also causally contribute to acute lung injury (ALI)/acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in susceptible patients,

9 manifesting as pulmonary interstitial and alveolar exudation with ground‐glass opacities (GGOs), reticular GGOs, mixed GGOs, patchy opacities, or consolidation in chest computed tomography (CT) images. Cases in which these imaging findings are localized to the lungs can be difficult to differentiate from pneumonia. 10 Furthermore, the common clinical symptoms of patients with acute PE are similar to those of patients with pneumonia, which often include chest pain, breathlessness, and fever. 11

Thus, according to the simplicity principle of initial diagnosis, patients with the aforementioned clinical symptoms who present with exudative lesions on chest CT images are more likely to be diagnosed with community‐acquired pneumonia (CAP). 12 , 13 However, if pneumonia‐like lung injury induced by inflammatory cytokines does indeed occur in acute PE, then a subset of patients with PE may be misdiagnosed with CAP, leading to treatment delays and even an increased risk of death.

We thus hypothesized that PE causes vascular endothelial damage resulting in extensive release of inflammatory factors, leading to focal lung injury in susceptible individuals and the appearance of pneumonia‐like findings. In view of this hypothesis, the present study analyzed chest CT images from a large sample of patients with PE or DVT to clarify the differences in the incidence of pneumonia lesions between the two groups. In addition, an animal model was established to verify whether PE rat plasma can lead to pneumonia‐like lung injury in healthy rats. METHODS Patient screening

Researchers were performed in the Hospital Information System (HIS) and digital scientific research platform of Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University using the following keywords: “pulmonary embolism,” “pulmonary thromboembolism,” “pulmonary arterial thromboembolism,” “PE,” “PTE,” “deep vein thrombosis,” “vein thrombosis,” and “DVT” to screen for hospitalized patients with a confirmed diagnosis of acute PE or DVT between January 2012 and September 2021. The inclusion criteria for the PE group were as follows: (1) patients aged ≥ 18 years and (2) CT pulmonary angiography findings consistent with acute PE. 14

The exclusion criteria for the PE group were as follows: (1) concomitant chest trauma; (2) multiple pulmonary metastatic foci; (3) left ventricular dysfunction; and (4) confirmed ALI. The inclusion criteria for the DVT group were as follows: (1) patients aged ≥ 18 years and (2) findings of ultrasonography of the lower extremity veins consistent with DVT. 15 , 16

The exclusion criteria for the DVT group were as follows: (1) concomitant chest trauma; (2) multiple pulmonary metastatic foci; (3) left ventricular dysfunction; (4) confirmed ALI; and (5) concomitant PE. We used the hospital's electronic registry to gather baseline information on demographics and comorbidities. The study was approved by the Ethical Committee of Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University (approval permit number: 2021PS859K). CT evaluation of pneumonia CT findings of pneumonia included light patchy opacity, GGO, reticular GGO, mixed GGO, patchy opacity, or consolidation (Figure 1 ). 17

Two trained researchers independently analyzed the CT images of the selected patients based on the present study criteria. The researchers were only informed of the imaging number and were not allowed to view the mediastinal window. The date of CT examination was from 2 weeks before to 5 days after the diagnosis of PE or DVT. Patients in the DVT group who did not receive chest CT during the scheduled period were analyzed separately. Figure 1. Open in a new tab Pneumonia lesions in lung computed tomographic (CT) image. (I) Light patchy opacities; (II) reticular ground‐glass opacities (GGOs); (III) mixed GGOs; (IV) GGOs; (V) patchy opacities; (VI) consolidation. “→” indicates pneumonia lesions.

Rat model and specimen collection The animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC) of Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University (approval permit number: 2020PS580K). Healthy 7‐week‐old male Sprague Dawley rats weighing 210–230 g purchased from Beijing HFK Bioscience Co. Ltd. were housed in cages under specific pathogen‐free conditions. Food and water were provided ad libitum.

At least five rats per group per timepoint were randomly assigned to the PE, PE‐control (PE‐con), PE plasma, and PE‐con plasma groups. To establish PE model, the rats were anesthetized intraperitoneally with 20% urethane at a dosage of 1400 mg/kg. The bilateral jugular veins were dissected. The right jugular vein was cannulated with a catheter connected to a pressure transducer, which was carefully inserted into the right ventricle to monitor right ventricular pressure. A needle for clots infusion was inserted into the left jugular vein. The clots were prepared 1 day before the operation. Blood was drawn from the rat tail vein and filled with a 0.5 mm diameter catheter, allowing natural coagulation to form thromboembolus. The rats were infused with 20 autologous clots 1 × 1 × 2 mm in size slowly over 5 min. A right ventricular pressure increase exceeding 10 mmHg above baseline pressure after clots infusion was considered as acute PE.

18 , 19 For few rats, supplementary clots were infused to take the right ventricular pressure exceeding that level. Not eligible for further experiment if the increase of right ventricular pressure did not reach 10 mmHg after the supplemental clot injection. The PE‐con group was injected with an equal volume of normal saline instead of clots.

Two hours after PE and PE‐con model establishment, blood was collected from the abdominal aorta. PE or PE‐con plasma were isolated via centrifugation and stored at −80°C. Healthy rats were injected via the tail vein with 1 mL of plasma from the PE or PE‐con groups to establish the groups of PE plasma or PE‐con plasma. Lung tissues were histologically assessed at 2 h for the PE and PE‐con groups, and at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8 h for the PE plasma and PE‐con plasma groups, respectively. Histological assessment Based on the American Thoracic Society (ATS) assessment method for ALI in animal models,

20 images were acquired using light microscopy under ×400, ×200, and ×40 magnification. Under a ×400 high‐power field, at least 20 fields of view were randomly selected while avoiding the predominance of the lumen of large airways or vessels to ensure that >50% of each field was occupied by lung alveoli. The mean value for overall lung injury scores was recorded as the total lung injury score (see Supplementary Table S1 ). The score in the most severe lung injury region was recorded as the highest lung injury score to determine whether focal lung injury occurred. The scale with the highest lung injury score >0.50, 0.70, or ≤0.30 was considered as proven lung injury, severe lung injury, or normal lungs, respectively.

21 Measurement of lung fluid content The accessory lobe of the right lung was carefully excised, and the wet weight was measured. Lung tissue was placed in a 60°C hot‐air oven and dried for 72 h, followed by measurement of dry weight. The wet/dry ratio was calculated to evaluate the degree of pulmonary edema. Statistical analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.01 and IBM SPSS Statistics 24.0. The Grubbs test was used for outliers, and two datapoints of the wet/dry ratio were rejected at the α = 0.05 significance level. All continuous values are expressed as the mean ± SEM. Data were assessed for normality by the Shapiro‒Wilk test. Student's t test was used to compare mean differences of normally distributed values. The Mann‒Whitney U test was used for skewed distributions. Binary variables were compared using the χ 2 test and Fisher's exact test. Data were considered statistically significant at two‐tailed p < 0.05. RESULTS
Comparison of pneumonia lesion incidence between the PE and DVT groups

After screening, 793 and 1773 eligible patients were enrolled in the PE and DVT groups, respectively. Among these, 859 patients (48.4%) in the DVT group were unavailable to obtain chest CT images. A total of 793 patients in the PE group and 914 patients in the DVT group were focused in this study. Table 1 shows the baseline clinical characteristics of the study patients. There was no statistical difference between PE and DVT groups regarding gender, age, nonrespiratory infectious diseases, cancers, and common chronic medical diseases. Significant differences were observed between PE and DVT groups in terms of connective tissue disease, trauma, and surgery. Table 1.

Previous studies have suggested that chronic lung disease, chronic digestive disease, trauma, and tumors could induce pulmonary inflammation. 22 , 23 , 24 , 25

In our study, only connective tissue disease, trauma, and surgery exhibited significantly higher incidence rates in the DVT group compared to the PE group. Nevertheless, this difference does not provide an explanation for the higher rate of pneumonia lesions observed in the PE group, which could potentially be attributed to PE. Table 2. Rat PE model establishment After injection of the thromboembolus, an immediate rise in right ventricular pressure of >10 mmHg was observed. At 2 h after injection, cyanosis was observed on the lips of PE rats. Lung tissue dissection revealed thromboembolism of the pulmonary artery, indicating successful establishment of the rat PE model (see Supplementary Figure S1 ). Proved lung injury in rat PE models

Gross specimen examination revealed spotted patterns on the surface of lung tissues of individuals in the PE group, whereas the lung tissues of the PE‐con group were uniformly pink (Figure 2a,d ). Haematoxylin‐eosin (HE) staining revealed focal pathological damage in the PE group, with the majority of injury sites located at the lung periphery (Figure 2b ). Significant thickening of the alveolar wall was observed at these sites with a large amount of inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly neutrophils), some neutrophils migrating into the alveolar space, and occasional fibrin exudation forming fibrin chains or hyaline membranes (Figure 2c ). The lung in PE‐con group was characterized by thin alveolar walls with few neutrophils (Figure 2e,f ). These observations suggested the occurrence of focal lung injury in PE rats,
20 which was also similar to CAP pathological damage. 26

The total lung injury score was significantly higher in the PE group than in the PE‐con group (0.41 ± 0.01 vs. 0.20 ± 0.01, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3a ). In the PE group, 88.9% (8/9) of rats exhibited proven lung injury (highest lung injury score > 0.50), of which 33.3% had severe lung injury (highest lung injury score > 0.70) and 1/9 had a highest lung injury score of 0.50. In the PE‐con group, none of the rats had proven lung injury (5/8 had a highest lung injury score ≤ 0.30, and 3/8 had a highest lung injury score of 0.37–0.48). The difference between the two groups was statistically significant ( p < 0.0001) (Table 3 ). None of the rats showed alveolar hemorrhage or lung tissue necrosis in either group. The wet/dry ratio was significantly higher in the PE group than in the PE‐con group (4.98 ± 0.08 vs. 4.39 ± 0.06, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3b ), implying more exudate in the lungs of PE rats.

Plasma of PE rats induced proved lung injury in the healthy

At 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8 h after healthy rats were infused with plasma from the PE rats (PE plasma group) or PE‐con rats (PE‐con plasma group), the gross lung tissue specimens exhibited similar findings to those of the PE and PE‐con groups (Figure 4a,b,d,e ). In the PE plasma group, focal pathological damage was observed at every experimental point individually (Figure 4c ), and most injury sites were located at the periphery of lung tissues (Figure 4b ). Similar to PE rats, these injury sites manifested as significant thickening of the alveolar wall, accompanied by neutrophil infiltration and occasional formation of fibrin chains or hyaline membranes (Figure 4b,c ). None of the rats in the PE‐con plasma group exhibited this damage (Figure 4e,f ). The total lung injury score was significantly higher in the PE plasma group than in the PE‐con plasma group at 0.5 and 4 h ( p < 0.05) (0.29 ± 0.03 vs. 0.19 ± 0.01 and 0.28 ± 0.03 vs. 0.17 ± 0.01, respectively) (Figure 5a ). In the PE plasma group, proven lung injury (highest lung injury score > 0.50) was observed in 8/29 (27.6%) rats, one of which exhibited severe lung injury (highest lung injury score = 0.82). In the PE‐con plasma group, none of the rats had proven lung injury (30.0% had a highest lung injury score ≤ 0.30, and 70.0% had a highest lung injury score of 0.32–0.48). The difference between the two groups was statistically significant ( p < 0.05) (Table 4 ). None of the rats showed alveolar hemorrhage or lung tissue necrosis in either group. The wet/dry ratio was significantly higher in the PE plasma group than in the PE‐con plasma group at 1 and 2 h (5.02 ± 0.12 vs. 4.61 ± 0.06 and 4.76 ± 0.16 vs. 4.34 ± 0.09, respectively; p < 0.05) (Figure 5b ), implying more lung exudate in the PE plasma group.

Patients with PE tend to be older and have multiple medical problems such as chronic lung disease, trauma, and so forth, which complicated the etiology of pulmonary inflammation. In contrast to patients with PE, the young rats with no comorbidities were used to animal study, thereby minimizing confounding factors that contribute to lung inflammation. The only reason for PE plasma group showing pneumonia‐like lung injury should be the infusion of PE plasma. Certain specific molecule induced by acute PE could trigger pneumonia‐like lung injury. DISCUSSION PE and DVT share common risk factors, including pulmonary infection. 27

The underlying mechanisms may involve inflammation‐induced vascular endothelial dysfunction. 28 Our study demonstrated that the incidence of PE or DVT with comorbid pneumonia based on CT images was 36.9% or 26.3%, respectively, and this difference was statistically significant. Similar conclusions were drawn by other studies regarding the inconsistency in pneumonia incidence between PE and DVT. 4

In the present study, appropriate CT images were unavailable for 48.4% of patients with DVT to evaluate for pneumonia. This may have led to a bias in the DVT group. However, given that chest CT scans are predominantly driven by respiratory symptoms, including pneumonia, patients without CT images might be less likely to have pneumonia than those with chest CT scans. Since PE and DVT share common risk factors, pneumonia as a trigger should theoretically have a similar incidence among both PE and DVT groups. A higher incidence of pneumonia lesions on CT images in PE than in DVT implies the involvement of other confounding factors. We realized that pulmonary infarction might be incorrectly accounted for as “pneumonia,” resulting in false positives in the PE group. However, we did not find any PE rats showing alveolar hemorrhage or lung tissue necrosis in the present study.

In the present study, we designed an animal experiment involving the injection of plasma from PE rats into healthy rats. Our findings revealed that some recipients of PE plasma showed focal pathological damage of proven lung injury (predominantly distributed at the lung periphery), which was observed at all experimental points after PE plasma injections. The total incidence of proven lung injury in the PE plasma group was 27.6%, of which 3.4% was severe lung injury, manifesting as significant thickening of the alveolar wall accompanied by a large amount of neutrophil infiltration, a small amount of neutrophil migration into the alveolar space, and occasional fibrin exudation. None of the rats were found to have alveolar hemorrhage or lung tissue necrosis in the PE group or PE plasma group. It is well known that PE may produce numerous cytokines and chemokines, such as interferon‐γ, IL‐6, IL‐8, IL‐9, IL‐10, IL‐1β, chemokine ligand 2, IL‐17A, transforming growth factor‐β, and TNF‐α,

7 many of which are also major inflammatory cytokines inducing ALI/ARDS. 9 , 29 Given that ARDS is inducible by extrapulmonary diseases, the lungs of susceptible individuals are target organs of systemic inflammatory factors. Animal experiments have demonstrated that the simulation of PE via the injection of polystyrene microspheres into the jugular vein (circulatory system) resulted in extensive recruitment of chemokines in lung tissues and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (respiratory tract). 30

These findings imply that the lungs of susceptible rats were indeed the target organs of the systemic inflammatory response induced by PE. Unfortunately, even if we do repeat previous experiments and confirm an increased level in some of these inflammatory cytokines in our PE model rats, we still cannot confirm they are correlated to ALI or not. However, determining which specific inflammatory cytokines are responsible for the lung injury is beyond the scope of this study's objectives. Collectively, these events resulted in similar pneumonia‐like pathological damage and might also correspond to the findings of GGO, 26 mixed GGO and reticular GGO observed in chest CT images. 31

Unlike the diffuse pathological damage of classic ALI/ARDS, PE‐induced lung injury had a focal distribution, which more closely resembled the distribution of lesions in patients with CAP. Therefore, the results of these animal experiments suggest that the possibility of PE diagnosis should be considered when patients exhibit acute onset of symptoms such as chest tightness, breathlessness, chest pain, and/or fever, which are accompanied by pneumonia lesions predominantly distributed in the lung periphery in chest images. Given that the treatment strategies for CAP and PE completely differ and that the efficacy of CAP treatment requires evaluation after 72 h, misdiagnosis of pneumonia‐like lesions caused by PE as CAP will result in a delay in PE diagnosis and may lead to adverse consequences. In addition, given that lung injury is caused by PE‐induced systemic inflammatory responses and that heightened systemic inflammatory responses are a major factor contributing to poor PE prognosis,
32 fully recognizing that patients with PE may exhibit pneumonia‐like lesions is essential to improving PE prognosis.

In our study, the researchers who reviewed images were well trained with the study criteria. They were blinded to PE status to minimize bias of the review results. To prevent overlooking patients in the early stages of pneumonia, patients with “mild” imaging findings were also included. Furthermore, to ensure that pneumonia might be a risk factor for venous thromboembolism, the time window for chest CT scans was defined as from 2 weeks before to 5 days after the diagnosis of PE or DVT. In the animal experiment, the PE plasma collection time (2 h after PE model establishment) was determined based on pilot data. The PE‐con group received an equivalent volume of normal saline that was injected via the jugular vein, and plasma was collected at the same time point as that for the PE group for injection into the PE‐con plasma group to eliminate the inflammatory effects caused by surgical trauma. The assessment method for animal models of lung injury was based on the recommendations of the ATS,

20 while the score thresholds for proven lung injury have been adopted in other studies. 21 We acknowledge certain limitations of the present study. As the patient population was retrospectively evaluated, most DVT patients lacked chest CT images acquired during the appropriate time window, which affected the accuracy of pneumonia incidence. The purpose of this study was to observe the possibility of PE plasma‐induced lung injury, and hence, only one experimental point was included to observe the pathological damage in both the PE group and PE‐con group. This could have underpinned the lack of evidence of pulmonary infarction.

In conclusion, the manifestation of pneumonia lesions in chest CT images was higher among PE patients than among DVT patients. Most PE rats developed focal proven lung injury, and some exhibited severe lung injury, manifesting as pneumonia‐like interstitial and alveolar exudation predominantly distributed at the lung periphery. These injuries are associated with the presence of PE‐induced pathogenic factors in the plasma, but further investigations are warranted to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. AUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONS

Pulmonary embolism (PE) is increasingly recognized as an episode of care that extends well beyond hospital discharge. Current guidance is distributed across several documents: the 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines; the 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) multisociety guideline, which replaced the massive/submassive terminology with clinical categories A–E; and separate position papers on catheter-directed intervention (CDI) and on follow-up. This narrative review (i) provides a side-by-side comparison of the ESC and AHA/ACC risk frameworks and their therapeutic implications; (ii) updates the evidence on reperfusion, including the recent randomized trials HI-PEITHO, PEERLESS and STORM-PE; and (iii) focuses on transitions of care and long-term follow-up, which guidelines address less comprehensively. Anticoagulation, preferably with a direct oral anticoagulant, remains the treatment for most patients. Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk (ESC) or category E (AHA/ACC) PE, because in intermediate-risk disease it halves hemodynamic decompensation at the cost of a several-fold increase in major and intracranial bleeding, without long-term functional benefit. In HI-PEITHO, ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed thrombolysis reduced a 7-day composite outcome driven by cardiorespiratory decompensation (4.0% vs. 10.3%) in intermediate-high-risk patients with additional markers of physiological stress, without intracranial hemorrhage; a survival benefit of CDI has not been demonstrated. At discharge, a minimum bundle should specify the drug, dose, anticipated duration, provoking context, bleeding mitigation and follow-up ownership, followed by early contact within one week and a structured review at approximately three months. Up to half of survivors report persistent dyspnea or exercise limitation, whereas chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) develops in approximately 2%–3%. Persistent symptoms should prompt phenotype-directed evaluation with echocardiography, ventilation/perfusion scintigraphy, cardiopulmonary exercise testing and, when indicated, right-heart catheterization interpreted with the 2022 hemodynamic definitions, followed by early referral to an expert center where pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty and medical therapy can be combined. We state the type of evidence underpinning each key recommendation, propose a discharge bundle, a structured follow-up algorithm and episode-wide quality indicators, and identify the evidence gaps that should guide future trials.

Keywords: anticoagulation, catheter-directed intervention, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, post-pulmonary embolism syndrome, pulmonary embolism, risk stratification, thrombolysis, venous thromboembolism 1. Introduction

Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome after myocardial infarction and stroke, with an annual incidence of approximately 39–115 per 100,000 population ( 1 ). Although age-standardized PE-related mortality in the European Union approximately halved between 2000 and 2015 ( 2 ), PE remains associated with early death, recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE), treatment-related bleeding and substantial post-acute morbidity ( 1 , 3 , 4 ).

The care gap increasingly lies after initial survival. Up to half of patients report persistent dyspnea, reduced exercise capacity or impaired quality of life months after the index event ( 5 , 6 ), and in the prospective FOCUS cohort the two-year cumulative incidence of post-PE impairment was 16.0% ( 7 ). Only a minority develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), but distinguishing deconditioning, comorbidity, persistent right ventricular (RV) dysfunction, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD) and CTEPH requires a structured pathway, and fragmented follow-up delays the diagnosis of operable disease ( 4 , 8 ).

Several authoritative documents already address parts of this pathway ( Table 1 ). The 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines ( 1 ) and the 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) multisociety guideline ( 9 ) cover diagnosis, risk stratification and acute treatment; the 2022 ESC position paper on follow-up ( 4 ) and the European Respiratory Society (ERS) statement on CTEPH ( 8 ) cover the post-acute phase; the 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines define the hemodynamic thresholds ( 10 ); and recent consensus documents address catheter-directed interventions ( 11 , 12 ). The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline itself spans diagnosis through follow-up, but these documents were developed in parallel and use different terminology—most visibly the ESC four-tier risk model versus the AHA/ACC clinical categories A–E—and a systematic comparison of international guidelines has identified areas of harmony, dissonance and silence, including the absence of a universal definition of shock in PE ( 13 ). The contribution of this review is therefore not to restate guideline recommendations, but to provide three elements that are not available in any single document: (i) an explicit side-by-side comparison of the European and American risk frameworks, with particular attention to the clinical implications of the new categories C–E, including incipient cardiopulmonary failure and normotensive shock; (ii) an evidence-graded update of acute reperfusion, incorporating the randomized trials of catheter-directed intervention (CDI) published since 2022 and stating the type of evidence that supports each key recommendation; and (iii) an operational framework linking acute decisions to longitudinal follow-up, consisting of a minimum discharge bundle with an acute-phase handover dataset, a phenotype-directed post-PE pathway and episode-wide quality indicators. The integrated pathway is summarized in the central illustration ( Figure 1 ).

2. Materials and methods

PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English-language publications in adults from 1 January 2000 to 31 August 2026, complemented by the websites of major cardiovascular, hematology, emergency medicine and respiratory societies for guidelines and consensus documents, and by ClinicalTrials.gov for ongoing randomized trials. The search combined “pulmonary embolism” or “venous thromboembolism” with terms for each domain of the review (diagnosis, risk stratification, anticoagulation, thrombolysis, catheter-directed intervention, mechanical thrombectomy, embolectomy, extracorporeal support, response teams, follow-up, post-pulmonary embolism syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease and hypertension, balloon pulmonary angioplasty and rehabilitation); the full search strings are provided in Supplementary Table S1 . Because generic terms failed to retrieve some recent trials in the initial search, the search was repeated during revision and supplemented by searches for the names of individual trials and registries ( Supplementary Table S1 ), forward citation tracking of the 2026 AHA/ACC guideline and the 2022 ESC follow-up position paper, and screening of the reference lists of key publications.

Eligible sources were, in descending order of priority, clinical practice guidelines and society consensus documents, randomized controlled trials and their meta-analyses, prospective cohort and management studies, and large registries; smaller observational studies were included only when higher-level evidence was lacking. Case reports, conference abstracts and unpublished data were excluded. Because the review was intended to integrate clinical practice rather than to estimate pooled effects, appraisal was qualitative and no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed. To make the evidence hierarchy explicit, the type of evidence supporting each key recommendation is stated in the text and summarized in Section 11 , and statements for which no supporting evidence was identified are labeled as the authors' opinion.
3. Pathophysiology across the acute-to-chronic continuum 3.1. Thrombus formation and provoking context

Most pulmonary emboli originate in the deep veins of the lower limbs or pelvis, reflecting a variable combination of venous stasis, endothelial perturbation and hypercoagulability ( 1 ). A major operation creates a strong exposure that disappears, whereas cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, chronic inflammatory disease or persistent immobility continue to generate risk; acute infection and critical illness act mainly as transient provoking factors ( 14 ). Because the provoking context determines the risk of recurrence once anticoagulation stops, it should be recorded precisely rather than reduced to the labels “provoked” and “unprovoked” ( 14 , 15 ).
3.2. Right ventricular failure and normotensive shock

Clinical severity is determined by the interaction between embolic obstruction and the capacity of the RV to adapt, rather than by the anatomical extent of obstruction alone ( 1 , 9 ). Acute pressure overload produces RV dilatation, increased wall stress and oxygen demand, septal displacement with reduced left ventricular filling and, through systemic hypotension, a lower right coronary perfusion gradient, initiating a self-reinforcing cycle of RV ischemia and failure ( 1 ). This explains why patients with limited reserve may decompensate after a smaller embolus, and why the AHA/ACC guideline advises against using thrombus burden for risk stratification ( 9 ). Compensatory vasoconstriction can maintain systolic pressure despite falling cardiac output, producing normotensive shock with rising lactate, oliguria or altered mentation; an elevated plasma lactate in normotensive patients is independently associated with adverse short-term outcomes ( 16 ). Hypoxemia results from ventilation/perfusion mismatch, low mixed venous oxygen saturation and, occasionally, right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale, so oxygen saturation is not a stand-alone measure of embolic severity ( 1 ).

3.3. From acute embolus to chronic thromboembolic disease In most patients, thrombus resolves substantially during the first months of anticoagulation. In a minority, organized thrombus becomes incorporated into the arterial wall as webs, bands, stenoses, pouch lesions and occlusions; flow is redistributed and a secondary small-vessel arteriopathy can develop in unobstructed territories, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) ( 8 , 17 ). The RV initially adapts through hypertrophy and later decompensates as reserve is exhausted. Because symptoms evolve gradually, chronic disease is frequently recognized late, which is the rationale for structured follow-up after acute PE ( 4 , 8 ).
4. Diagnosis 4.1. Pre-test probability and D-dimer

Diagnostic testing should begin with explicit estimation of clinical probability ( 1 , 9 ). In patients with low or intermediate pre-test probability, a negative highly sensitive D-dimer safely excludes PE. An age-adjusted threshold (age × 10 µg/L above 50 years) increased the proportion of patients aged ≥75 years in whom PE could be excluded from 6.4% to 29.7%, with a three-month failure rate of 0.3% ( 18 ). The YEARS strategy, which combines three clinical items with probability-adapted D-dimer thresholds, avoided computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) in 48% of patients, compared with 34% under the conventional algorithm, with a three-month VTE rate of 0.61% among patients in whom PE was excluded without imaging ( 19 ). The pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC) are appropriate only in patients with very low clinical probability; in this population the PROPER cluster-randomized trial showed non-inferiority, with a three-month VTE rate of 0.1% ( 20 ). A pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm avoided CTPA in 39% of pregnant women with a three-month VTE rate of 0.21% ( 21 ). A positive D-dimer is not diagnostic and is particularly nonspecific in hospitalized patients, cancer, pregnancy, infection and advanced age; infection and critical illness also elevate troponin and natriuretic peptides, which should be considered when these biomarkers are used for risk stratification ( 1 ).
4.2. Imaging strategy

CTPA is the reference imaging test for most adults because it confirms emboli, depicts RV enlargement and may identify alternative diagnoses ( 1 , 9 ). Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy remains important when iodinated contrast is contraindicated, when radiation to breast tissue is a major concern (for example, in young women and during pregnancy), and when chronic thromboembolic obstruction is suspected ( 1 , 22 ). Compression ultrasonography can establish VTE when proximal deep-vein thrombosis (DVT) is demonstrated, but a negative examination does not exclude PE. Bedside echocardiography is not a rule-out test in stable patients; in shock, however, acute RV pressure overload can justify immediate reperfusion when transport to definitive imaging is unsafe ( 1 ). The principal diagnostic tools are summarized in Table 2 . CTPA also provides early clues to pre-existing chronic disease—eccentric wall-adherent defects, webs, bands, mosaic perfusion or enlarged bronchial arteries—which should be reported because they change the follow-up plan ( 8 , 10 ).

Incidental and isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism

The AHA/ACC guideline assigns asymptomatic, incidentally detected PE to a separate category A ( 9 ). Incidental PE detected during cancer staging carries a meaningful recurrence risk and is treated like symptomatic PE when segmental or more proximal ( 23 , 24 ). Isolated subsegmental PE is more difficult, because small defects are susceptible to artifact while treatment exposes patients with a low absolute recurrence risk to bleeding. In a prospective management study of 266 patients with subsegmental PE and no proximal DVT managed without anticoagulation, the 90-day rate of recurrent VTE was 3.1%, higher than anticipated, with a higher rate among patients with multiple subsegmental defects ( 25 ). On this evidence, surveillance without anticoagulation is defensible only for a single subsegmental defect confirmed by expert review, with negative bilateral proximal ultrasonography, adequate cardiopulmonary reserve, no active cancer or other persistent risk factor, and assured follow-up; multiple defects, reduced reserve, ongoing risk factors or inability to provide surveillance favor anticoagulation ( 1 , 3 , 25 , 26 ).
5. Risk stratification: European and American frameworks 5.1. The 2019 ESC model

The ESC model first identifies high-risk PE, defined by hemodynamic instability: cardiac arrest, obstructive shock [systolic blood pressure (SBP) < 90 mmHg or vasopressor requirement with end-organ hypoperfusion], or persistent hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or a drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min not explained by other causes) ( 1 ). Normotensive patients are then classified using the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) ( 27 ) or its simplified version (sPESI), RV dysfunction on echocardiography or CTPA, and cardiac troponin. Intermediate-high risk requires both RV dysfunction and an elevated troponin; intermediate-low risk applies when one or neither is present in a patient with PESI class III–V or sPESI ≥1, or when either is present despite a low clinical score; low risk requires a low clinical score without RV dysfunction or troponin elevation when these are assessed ( 1 ). Quantitatively, sPESI 0 identified a 30-day mortality of 1.0% versus 10.9% for sPESI ≥1 ( 28 ), and elevated troponin was associated with a more than five-fold increase in short-term mortality (odds ratio 5.24) ( 29 ). The Hestia criteria address a different question, namely whether home treatment is feasible (Section 7.1 ) ( 30 ).
5.2. The 2026 AHA/ACC clinical categories

The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline abandoned the terms massive and submassive and introduced five clinical categories with subcategories ( Table 3 ) ( 9 ): A, subclinical (incidental, asymptomatic) PE; B, symptomatic PE with a low severity score (sPESI 0, PESI ≤85 or Bova ≤4); C, symptomatic PE with an elevated score, subdivided by RV imaging and biomarkers (troponin, natriuretic peptide or lactate) into C1 (both normal), C2 (abnormal RV or biomarker) and C3 (abnormal RV and biomarker); D, incipient cardiopulmonary failure, comprising D1 (transient, fluid-responsive hypotension <15 min) and D2 (normotensive shock, for example lactate >2 mmol/L, oliguria or altered mentation); and E, cardiopulmonary failure, comprising E1 (persistent hypotension with cardiogenic shock) and E2 (refractory shock or cardiac arrest). A respiratory modifier (“R”) is added to categories C–E when hypoxemia, tachypnea or an escalating oxygen requirement is present ( 9 ).

5.3. Side-by-side comparison

The correspondence between the frameworks ( Table 3 ) is approximate: categories A and B broadly correspond to ESC low-risk PE; C1 and C2 to intermediate-low risk; and C3, D1 and D2 to intermediate-high risk ( 1 , 9 ). The most important difference lies at the boundary between intermediate- and high-risk disease: patients with transient hypotension (D1) or normotensive shock (D2) represent a more severe stage than C3, but they remain within the ESC intermediate-high-risk class, because the ESC model reserves high risk for cardiac arrest, obstructive shock or persistent hypotension, whereas the AHA/ACC framework recognizes them as a distinct, threatened group in which reperfusion “may be considered” ( 9 ). The AHA/ACC framework also makes lactate measurement (Class 1 in categories C–E), the respiratory modifier and incidental PE explicit, and recommends multidisciplinary PE response team (PERT) evaluation for categories C–E ( 9 ). Conversely, the principles are convergent: hemodynamic status defines urgency, RV dysfunction and myocardial injury refine prognosis in normotensive patients, routine systemic thrombolysis is not recommended in normotensive patients without signs of deterioration, and outpatient care is appropriate for selected low-risk patients ( 1 , 9 ). Clinical implications of categories C, D and E

Category C comprises hospitalized patients who rarely benefit from therapies beyond anticoagulation; its subdivision by RV imaging and biomarkers, with lactate measurement (Class 1), is intended to identify those at risk of progression ( 9 ). Category C3, particularly with a respiratory modifier, resembles the PEITHO and HI-PEITHO populations, in whom the role of CDI is debated (Section 6.5 ) ( 31 , 32 ).

Category D is the main conceptual advance of the 2026 framework. It recognizes incipient cardiopulmonary failure in patients whose blood pressure is not persistently low: transient, fluid-responsive hypotension (D1) and normotensive shock (D2), defined by markers of hypoperfusion such as lactate >2 mmol/L, acute kidney injury, oliguria, altered mentation or a cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m 2 ( 9 ). In the FLASH registry, approximately one-third of normotensive patients with intermediate-risk PE who underwent invasive hemodynamic assessment had a cardiac index in the shock range ( 33 ), and a composite shock score combining clinical, biochemical and imaging variables has been proposed to identify them non-invasively ( 34 ). Clinically, category D implies admission to an intensive care or high-dependency unit, immediate PERT involvement, avoidance of sedation, intubation and aggressive fluid loading, early vasopressor or inotropic support, and readiness for reperfusion, for which the AHA/ACC guideline assigns a Class 2b recommendation ( 9 ). The evidence base is, however, limited: the concept derives largely from retrospective analyses of patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, and no prospective study has yet shown that treating normotensive shock differently improves outcomes ( 9 , 33 ).

Category E corresponds to ESC high-risk PE and mandates immediate reperfusion and circulatory support; by distinguishing refractory shock or arrest (E2), the framework specifies when VA-ECMO is reasonable and surgery without circulatory support is not preferred (Sections 6.3 and 6.6) ( 1 , 9 ). 5.5. Translating categories into monitoring and escalation

A single baseline label is insufficient because patients may progress from stable RV strain to incipient failure, a trajectory formalized by the AHA/ACC D categories ( 9 ). In the authors' opinion, the admission note of every patient at ESC intermediate-high risk or in AHA/ACC category C3–D should document explicit escalation triggers (new hypotension, rising lactate, increasing oxygen requirement, syncope, altered mentation, oliguria, progressive tachycardia or worsening RV failure), the pre-agreed rescue strategy and the responsible team, consistent with the recommendation for PERT involvement in these categories ( 1 , 9 ). 6. Acute treatment 6.1. Initial stabilization

Supportive therapy should protect RV perfusion and avoid iatrogenic collapse. Because aggressive volume loading may worsen RV dilatation and left ventricular underfilling, cautious fluid administration (≤500 mL) is reserved for patients with low central venous pressure, and norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for hypotension ( 1 ). Induction of anesthesia and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate collapse by reducing venous return and increasing RV afterload; the AHA/ACC guideline therefore advises against deep sedation and intubation unless clinically necessary in patients with RV dysfunction ( 1 , 9 ). Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) may stabilize refractory shock or cardiac arrest as a bridge to reperfusion or recovery, but it is not definitive thrombus therapy (Section 6.6 ) ( 9 , 35 ).
6.2. Anticoagulation

Anticoagulation should begin promptly, including while awaiting imaging when clinical probability is high or intermediate ( 1 ). Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is preferred over unfractionated heparin (UFH) for parenteral therapy in most patients because of more predictable pharmacokinetics and lower rates of recurrence without increased bleeding ( 1 , 9 ); UFH remains preferable when immediate reperfusion or another procedure is anticipated, when rapid reversal may be needed, and in severe renal impairment ( 1 ). For most eligible adults, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over vitamin K antagonists (VKAs). In a meta-analysis of the phase 3 trials, DOACs had similar efficacy for recurrent VTE [relative risk (RR) 0.90] and reduced major bleeding (RR 0.61), intracranial hemorrhage (RR 0.37) and fatal bleeding ( 36 – 40 ). Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be started without a parenteral lead-in, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban require at least five days of parenteral anticoagulation. In the randomized COBRRA trial, clinically relevant bleeding during three months of treatment was lower with apixaban than with rivaroxaban (3.3% vs. 7.1%; RR 0.46) ( 41 ).

Drug choice must account for renal and hepatic function, pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, body weight, interactions, adherence, affordability, cancer site, thrombocytopenia and planned procedures ( Table 5 ). In cancer-associated VTE, factor Xa inhibitors were non-inferior or superior to dalteparin for recurrence, but edoxaban and rivaroxaban increased gastrointestinal and genitourinary bleeding in patients with luminal tumors, whereas apixaban did not increase major bleeding (3.8% vs. 4.0%) ( 24 , 42 – 44 ). In high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome, rivaroxaban caused an excess of thrombotic and bleeding events compared with warfarin, and VKAs remain the agents of choice ( 45 ); recommendations for obesity and pregnancy are summarized in Table 5 ( 22 , 46 ).

Systemic thrombolysis

Systemic thrombolysis is recommended for high-risk PE (ESC Class I, level of evidence B; AHA/ACC category E, Class 2a) when bleeding risk is acceptable ( 1 , 9 ). In a meta-analysis of 16 trials, thrombolysis was associated with lower all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.53) but higher major bleeding (9.24% vs. 3.42%) and intracranial hemorrhage (1.46% vs. 0.19%) ( 47 ). In intermediate-high-risk PE, the PEITHO trial showed that full-dose tenecteplase reduced death or hemodynamic decompensation within 7 days (2.6% vs. 5.6%; odds ratio 0.44), but increased major extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs. 1.2%) and hemorrhagic stroke (2.0% vs. 0.2%), without a mortality advantage ( 32 ). Its long-term follow-up showed no benefit on survival, functional limitation or CTEPH (Section 9.2 ) ( 48 ). Accordingly, both guidelines recommend against routine systemic thrombolysis in normotensive patients (ESC Class III; AHA/ACC categories A–C2, Class 3: Harm) and favor anticoagulation with close monitoring and rescue reperfusion if deterioration occurs (ESC Class I for rescue thrombolysis) ( 1 , 9 ). For categories D1–D2, systemic thrombolysis “may be considered” (Class 2b) ( 9 ).

Reduced-dose thrombolysis is attractive: 50 mg of alteplase was as effective as 100 mg on radiological endpoints with fewer bleeding events ( 49 ), but such trials have been underpowered for clinical outcomes. The ongoing PEITHO-3 trial is randomizing approximately 650 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE and additional clinical markers of severity to reduced-dose alteplase or placebo on top of heparin, with a 30-day composite of death, hemodynamic decompensation or recurrent PE as the primary outcome ( 50 ). Contraindications should be weighed against the threat of imminent death from obstructive shock ( 1 ). 6.4. Catheter-directed intervention: terminology and evidence

For clarity, we use catheter-directed intervention (CDI) as an umbrella term for percutaneous reperfusion techniques, comprising two families ( 11 , 12 ). Local (catheter-directed) thrombolysis delivers a low total dose of fibrinolytic—typically 8–24 mg of alteplase over several hours—through standard multi-side-hole catheters (conventional catheter-directed thrombolysis, CDT) or ultrasound-facilitated catheters (USCDT). Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) removes thrombus without, or with minimal, fibrinolytic exposure, using large-bore aspiration or extraction systems or computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy. Early evidence consisted of single-arm studies or small randomized trials with surrogate endpoints, chiefly the reduction in the RV-to-left ventricular (RV/LV) diameter ratio at 24–48 h: ULTIMA, SEATTLE II, OPTALYSE and SUNSET sPE for local thrombolysis ( 51 – 54 ), and FLARE, EXTRACT-PE and the 800-patient FLASH registry for MT ( 55 – 57 ). In high-risk PE, the non-randomized FLAME study reported in-hospital mortality of 1.9% with large-bore MT versus 29.5% in a context arm treated predominantly with systemic thrombolysis, although the groups were not comparable, so these data represent observational evidence only ( 58 ). The small CANARY trial was stopped early without a significant difference in its primary endpoint ( 59 ) ( Table 7 ).

The evidence base has changed substantially with four randomized trials ( Table 7 ). HI-PEITHO randomized 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE (RV/LV ≥1.0, elevated troponin) and at least two markers of physiological stress (heart rate ≥100/min, SBP ≤110 mmHg, respiratory rate ≥20/min or oxygen saturation ≤90%) to USCDT plus anticoagulation or anticoagulation alone ( 31 ). The 7-day composite of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse, or symptomatic recurrence occurred in 4.0% versus 10.3% (RR 0.39; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.20–0.77), corresponding to a number needed to treat of approximately 16. The effect was driven by cardiorespiratory decompensation (3.7% vs. 10.3%), defined to include a National Early Warning Score ≥9; PE-related death (1.1% vs. 0.4%) and 30-day all-cause mortality (1.8% vs. 1.1%) did not differ, there was no intracranial hemorrhage, and 7-day major bleeding was numerically but not significantly higher (4.1% vs. 2.2%) ( 31 ). In PEERLESS (550 patients), large-bore MT was superior to CDT on a hierarchical win ratio (5.01; 95% CI 3.68–6.97) driven by less clinical deterioration or bailout (1.8% vs. 5.4%) and lower intensive care unit (ICU) use, without differences in mortality or bleeding ( 60 ). In STORM-PE (100 patients), computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy plus anticoagulation reduced the 48-hour RV/LV ratio more than anticoagulation alone (0.52 vs. 0.24) ( 61 ).

HI-PEITHO is thus the first adequately powered randomized trial to show that a CDI reduces early clinical deterioration. However, it was open-label and industry-funded, enrolled highly selected patients at experienced centers, relied on a composite in which a physiological score contributed substantially, and did not show reductions in mortality; long-term functional outcomes are pending ( 31 ). PEERLESS compared two interventional strategies with a resource-driven endpoint, and STORM-PE used a surrogate endpoint ( 60 , 61 ). Ongoing trials, including PEERLESS II (large-bore MT versus anticoagulation), PE-TRACT (CDI versus anticoagulation with functional endpoints) and PEITHO-3, will further define net benefit (Section 11 ).
6.5. Elective CDI in intermediate-high-risk PE with several adverse prognostic markers

Whether such patients should undergo elective CDI rather than anticoagulation with rescue therapy is the most debated question in acute PE care. Arguments in favor include the 61% relative reduction in early decompensation in HI-PEITHO ( 31 ), the low rates of intracranial hemorrhage with CDI compared with systemic thrombolysis ( 31 , 47 , 60 ), and the position statement of the Spanish Society of Cardiology, which suggests considering elective CDI within 24 h in intermediate-high-risk patients with multiple poor prognostic factors (for example, elevated lactate, syncope, borderline blood pressure or tachycardia) ( 12 ). The AHA/ACC guideline assigns a Class 2b recommendation (benefit unclear) to CDI in categories C2–C3 and “may be considered” in D1–D2 ( 9 ). Arguments for caution include the absence of a mortality benefit, the lack of long-term benefit after thrombolysis in PEITHO ( 48 ), procedural complications ( 12 , 62 ), costs, unequal access, and the fact that most patients treated with anticoagulation alone in HI-PEITHO and PEITHO did not deteriorate ( 31 , 32 ).

CDI-related complications can be grouped into access-site and vascular complications (hematoma, inadvertent arterial puncture, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula); bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage when a fibrinolytic is used; injury to the pulmonary arteries (perforation or pseudoaneurysm, presenting with hemoptysis, hemothorax or desaturation) or to the right heart (tricuspid valve damage, perforation or tamponade, and arrhythmias including atrioventricular block); periprocedural hemodynamic deterioration; and device-related problems such as catheter entrapment or kinking ( 62 ). Their reported frequency varies widely, because definitions are not standardized and reporting windows range from 48 h to 90 days ( 62 ). In the randomized trials and prospective registries summarized in a recent expert review, access-site complications occurred in approximately 1%–8% of patients, the overall rate of pulmonary artery injury was around 0.7%, and intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 0%–2% ( 62 ). Major bleeding ranged from approximately 1% with large-bore MT in the FLASH registry to approximately 7% with either MT or CDT in PEERLESS and 10% with USCDT in SEATTLE II, and it reached 11% after MT in high-risk patients in FLAME ( 54 , 55 , 58 , 60 ). Randomized trials report no or very low procedural mortality, whereas real-world data report CDI-related mortality of 3.5%–6.7%, and in the US Food and Drug Administration Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database, pulmonary vascular perforation was the most common complication resulting in death after mechanical thrombectomy ( 62 ). Large-bore aspiration also entails blood loss, which is now mitigated by blood-return systems ( 12 ). These data support performing CDI at experienced centers, with real-time ultrasound-guided venous access, careful catheter and guidewire manipulation and predefined bail-out options such as systemic thrombolysis or surgery, and weighing the expected benefit against procedural risk in each patient ( 12 , 62 ).

Thus, the evidence supporting elective CDI consists of one randomized trial with an early clinical endpoint, surrogate-endpoint trials and registries, and expert consensus. In the authors' opinion, pending PEITHO-3, PEERLESS II and PE-TRACT, elective CDI is reasonable after PERT discussion for patients who meet HI-PEITHO-like criteria (ESC intermediate-high risk or AHA/ACC category C3 with at least two markers of physiological stress) or AHA/ACC category D1–D2, have low procedural risk and are treated at experienced centers; other normotensive patients should receive anticoagulation with monitoring and a predefined rescue strategy.
6.6. High-risk PE when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed

For high-risk PE with a contraindication to, or failure of, systemic thrombolysis, the ESC recommends surgical embolectomy (Class I, level C) and suggests percutaneous catheter-directed treatment as an alternative (Class IIa, level C) ( 1 ); the AHA/ACC guideline considers local thrombolysis, MT and surgical embolectomy reasonable in category E1 (Class 2a) and VA-ECMO reasonable in category E2 with refractory shock (Class 2a) ( 9 ). No randomized trial has compared MT with local thrombolysis in this setting, so their relative roles rest on mechanistic reasoning, registry data and expert consensus rather than on comparative trials ( 11 , 12 , 58 ). MT provides immediate debulking without fibrinolytic exposure and is generally preferred when the contraindication is absolute (for example, recent intracranial hemorrhage or active bleeding) or when the patient cannot await a multi-hour infusion; local thrombolysis, which still exposes the patient to a low-dose fibrinolytic, may be considered when contraindications are relative, when MT is unavailable, or after incomplete mechanical debulking ( 11 , 12 ). In refractory shock or cardiac arrest, VA-ECMO can serve as a bridge to MT or surgical embolectomy; observational case series suggest better outcomes when ECMO is combined with definitive reperfusion than when it is used as stand-alone therapy, but no randomized data exist ( 9 , 35 ).
6.7. Surgical embolectomy, right-heart thrombus and PE response teams

Surgical embolectomy is an option for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, and for thrombus in transit or straddling a patent foramen ovale ( 1 , 9 ); outcomes depend heavily on selection and experience, with an in-hospital mortality of 27.2% in a nationwide United States cohort ( 63 ). Evidence for surgical embolectomy is limited to observational series. Management of right-heart thrombus should be individualized by a multidisciplinary team according to hemodynamic status, thrombus mobility and size, bleeding risk, patent foramen ovale and local expertise, as randomized evidence is lacking ( 1 ). The AHA/ACC guideline recommends multidisciplinary PERT evaluation for categories C–E (Class 1) ( 9 ). This recommendation rests on observational before-and-after studies: in a meta-analysis, PERT implementation increased the use of advanced therapies (RR 2.67), whereas the reduction in mortality was not significant (RR 0.89; 95% CI 0.67–1.19) ( 64 , 65 ). A PERT should therefore be judged by timeliness, appropriateness, complications and patient-centered outcomes, not by procedural volume (authors' opinion).

6.8. Inferior vena cava filters Inferior vena cava filters do not treat PE. In PREPIC2, adding a retrievable filter to anticoagulation did not reduce recurrent PE at three months (3.0% vs. 1.5%; RR 2.00) ( 66 ). Filters should be reserved for acute VTE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrence despite adequate anticoagulation, with a documented retrieval plan ( 1 , 9 ). 7. Transitions of care: disposition, discharge and early follow-up 7.1. Outpatient treatment and early discharge

Selected low-risk patients (ESC low risk; AHA/ACC categories A–B) can be treated at home or discharged early ( 1 , 9 ). Outpatient treatment was non-inferior to inpatient care in the randomized OTPE trial (recurrent VTE 0.6% vs. 0% at 90 days) ( 67 ); early discharge on rivaroxaban was associated with recurrent VTE or PE-related death in 0.6% in HoT-PE ( 68 ); and in HOME-PE, Hestia- and sPESI-based triage yielded similar 30-day adverse outcomes (3.8% vs. 3.6%) ( 69 ). A low clinical score is necessary but not sufficient. Oxygen requirement, bleeding risk, renal function, comorbidity, pain control, medication access, health literacy and social support must also be favorable ( 30 , 69 ). In the authors' opinion, when medication access, housing, transport, language support or follow-up are unreliable, a brief admission may be safer than nominally guideline-concordant discharge.
7.2. The minimum discharge bundle

In the authors' experience, the most preventable anticoagulant errors occur at transitions: the initial high-dose phase of apixaban and rivaroxaban, the parenteral lead-in for dabigatran and edoxaban, VKA overlap, duplication with residual heparin and prescriptions that do not cover the initiation phase. We therefore propose a minimum discharge bundle ( Table 8 ) that specifies the drug, dose and date of any dose change, the provisional duration and provoking context, bleeding mitigation, warning signs and a named clinician responsible for follow-up. The bundle operationalizes the AHA/ACC recommendations for clinical contact within the first week after discharge (Class 1), a visit at or before three months to decide on anticoagulation duration (Class 1), and systematic enquiry about PE-related symptoms and functional limitation at every visit for at least one year (Class 1) ( 9 ), as well as the ESC recommendation for routine re-evaluation three to six months after acute PE (Class I) ( 1 , 4 ).

Planned interruptions should be scheduled rather than improvised: heparin bridging during DOAC interruption is unnecessary and increases bleeding ( 70 ), and, in the authors' opinion, elective procedures should be deferred until the initial treatment phase has been completed whenever possible. 7.3. Communication and shared decision-making

Shared decision-making is essential when evidence supports more than one reasonable strategy: surveillance versus anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE, finite versus extended therapy, reduced-dose secondary prevention, elective CDI, and intervention for symptomatic CTEPD without resting pulmonary hypertension ( 4 , 9 ). The AHA/ACC guideline considers screening for anxiety and depression reasonable (Class 2a) ( 9 ). In the authors' opinion, explaining hemodynamic risk and the expected recovery trajectory is more informative for patients than anatomical terms such as “massive”. 8. Duration of anticoagulation and secondary prevention 8.1. The duration decision

All patients require at least three months of therapeutic anticoagulation; thereafter, the decision balances the risk of recurrence if treatment stops, the risk of bleeding if it continues, and patient preference ( 1 , 9 ). After a first unprovoked VTE, the cumulative risk of recurrence after stopping anticoagulation is approximately 10% at one year, 16% at two years, 25% at five years and 36% at ten years ( 15 ). A major transient provoking factor, such as major surgery, supports discontinuation after three months, whereas unprovoked PE, persistent risk factors, active cancer and recurrent VTE favor extended therapy ( 1 , 14 , 26 , 71 ). The AHA/ACC guideline recommends continuing anticoagulation—with reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban as an option—after the initial three months unless the PE was a first event strongly provoked by a transient risk factor (Class 1) ( 9 ).

Reduced-dose DOACs combine efficacy with a favorable bleeding profile. In AMPLIFY-EXT, recurrent VTE or VTE-related death occurred in 8.8% with placebo versus 1.7% with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, with similar major bleeding ( 72 ); in EINSTEIN CHOICE, recurrence was 1.2% with rivaroxaban 10 mg versus 4.4% with aspirin ( 73 ). In RENOVE, which enrolled patients at high risk of recurrence, reduced-dose DOACs were non-inferior to full-dose DOACs for recurrent VTE (2.2% vs. 1.8%) and reduced clinically relevant bleeding (9.9% vs. 15.2%; hazard ratio 0.61) ( 74 ). In API-CAT, reduced-dose apixaban was non-inferior to full-dose apixaban for extended treatment of cancer-associated VTE (recurrence 2.1% vs. 2.8%), with less clinically relevant bleeding (12.1% vs. 15.6%) ( 75 ).

8.2. Dynamic reassessment of bleeding risk Bleeding risk is dynamic: age, kidney function, anemia, antiplatelet or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, uncontrolled hypertension, alcohol, falls and prior bleeding should be reviewed at each visit and modified where possible ( 1 , 4 ). In the authors' opinion, neither a previous PE nor a bleeding score should replace shared decision-making, and in older adults falls rarely justify withholding anticoagulation in isolation. 8.3. Special populations

In cancer-associated PE, thrombotic and bleeding risks vary with tumor site, mucosal involvement, anticancer therapy, thrombocytopenia and prognosis, and anticoagulation generally continues while cancer is active ( 24 ). Thrombocytopenia requires a graded strategy; full-dose anticoagulation is usually continued above 50 × 10⁹/L, whereas dose reduction, platelet support or temporary interruption are considered below this threshold depending on clot burden and time from the acute event ( 76 ). After estrogen-associated PE, estrogen-containing contraception is usually replaced by progestin-only or nonhormonal methods before anticoagulation ends; in an analysis of the EINSTEIN trials, continuing hormonal therapy during anticoagulation was not associated with an excess of recurrent VTE, whereas abnormal uterine bleeding was more frequent with rivaroxaban than with enoxaparin/VKA ( 77 ). Pregnancy-associated PE is treated with LMWH for at least six weeks postpartum and for a minimum total duration of three months, and future pregnancies require a prophylaxis plan ( 1 , 22 ). In severe or rapidly changing renal dysfunction, UFH may offer controllability, and DOAC selection must reflect drug clearance ( 1 ).

8.4. Suspected recurrence during anticoagulation Suspected recurrence requires objective confirmation and comparison with previous imaging, because residual abnormalities may persist ( 1 , 4 ). The evaluation should establish the drug and dose, adherence, interruptions, malabsorption, renal and hepatic function and interacting medication; when recurrence is confirmed despite verified exposure, cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia should be considered, and a temporary switch to LMWH is commonly used (authors' opinion). 9. Post-PE syndrome, CTEPD and CTEPH 9.1. Definitions and hemodynamic thresholds

The post-pulmonary embolism (post-PE) syndrome is an umbrella term for new or persistent dyspnea, exercise limitation or impaired quality of life after at least three months of adequate anticoagulation that is not explained by other conditions ( 4 , 5 ). It comprises distinct phenotypes ( Table 9 ): symptoms without demonstrable cardiopulmonary impairment, frequently related to deconditioning or dysfunctional breathing; post-PE cardiac impairment with persistent RV dysfunction; CTEPD without pulmonary hypertension; and CTEPH ( 4 ). According to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines, pulmonary hypertension is defined at right-heart catheterization by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg, and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension additionally requires a pulmonary arterial wedge pressure (PAWP) ≤ 15 mmHg and a PVR >2 Wood units (WU); exercise pulmonary hypertension is defined by an mPAP/cardiac output slope >3 mmHg/L/min between rest and exercise ( 10 ). CTEPH is pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with mismatched perfusion defects and imaging signs of chronic thromboembolic obstruction after at least three months of effective anticoagulation ( 8 , 10 ). CTEPD is the broader term for symptomatic patients with these perfusion defects and chronic thromboembolic changes, with or without pulmonary hypertension at rest ( 8 , 10 ).
9.2. Frequency and the effect of acute reperfusion

Persistent limitation is common. In the prospective ELOPE cohort, 46.6% of patients had a peak oxygen uptake below 80% of predicted one year after PE ( 6 ). In FOCUS, the two-year cumulative incidence of post-PE impairment was 16.0% and that of CTEPH 2.3%; post-PE impairment identified 15 of the 16 patients eventually diagnosed with CTEPH ( 7 ). A meta-analysis estimated the incidence of CTEPH at 0.56% in all-comers, 3.2% in survivors and 2.8% in survivors without major comorbidities ( 78 ), consistent with earlier prospective cohorts reporting 1.5% and 3.8% at two years ( 79 , 80 ). Reperfusion has not been shown to prevent chronic sequelae: in the three-year follow-up of PEITHO, tenecteplase did not reduce CTEPH (2.1% vs. 3.2%), persistent dyspnea or functional limitation (36.0% vs. 30.1%), or residual pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction on echocardiography ( 48 ). Whether CDI modifies long-term outcomes is unknown, and the long-term data of HI-PEITHO and PE-TRACT are awaited ( 31 ).

9.3. Structured follow-up and screening algorithms A visit at approximately three months is the clinical anchor of follow-up ( 1 , 4 , 9 ). The Post-VTE Functional Status (PVFS) scale and the disease-specific Pulmonary Embolism Quality of Life (PEmb-QoL) questionnaire allow standardized and serial assessment ( 81 , 82 ). Routine imaging of asymptomatic patients and screening for CTEPH in asymptomatic survivors are not recommended (ESC Class III) ( 1 ), whereas symptomatic patients with mismatched perfusion defects beyond three months should be referred to a pulmonary hypertension/CTEPH center (ESC Class I) ( 1 ).

The ESC position paper proposes echocardiography for patients with persistent dyspnea, functional limitation or CTEPH risk factors, followed by V/Q scintigraphy and referral when pulmonary hypertension is probable ( 4 ). In the InShape II management study (424 patients), an algorithm combining the CTEPH prediction score with electrocardiography and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) excluded CTEPH without echocardiography in 81% of patients, with a failure rate of 0.29% during two years, and identified 10 of the 13 CTEPH cases within four months ( 83 ). In InShape IV, adding a dedicated reading of the index CTPA for signs of chronic thromboembolism reduced the failure rate to 0%, with 20%–24% of patients requiring echocardiography ( 84 ), underlining the value of handing forward acute-phase imaging findings. A recent Delphi study among 39 European experts reached consensus that the three-month visit should assess the full spectrum of sequelae (CTEPH, CTEPD and post-PE syndrome) using patient-reported outcomes, that CPET is useful in persistent dyspnea, that right-heart catheterization belongs in specialized centers, that patients with persistent dyspnea need extended follow-up even after CTEPH and CTEPD are excluded, and that a single uniform protocol is preferable ( 85 , 86 ). Our pathway integrating these elements is shown in Figure 2 ; its screening components rest on prospective management studies, whereas visit timing and multidisciplinary organization rest on expert consensus ( 4 , 85 ).
